ocar.opportunity: Large human imaging projects such as the Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank map brain architecture and connectivity with non-invasive scans, but those maps are only as good as the imaging measures themselves.
ocar.challenge: True long-distance wiring cannot be checked with invasive tracers in humans, so it remains unclear how well fMRI “functional connectivity” and diffusion-MRI tractography match anatomical projections.
ocar.action: Hayashi and colleagues describe the NonHuman Primate Neuroimaging & Neuroanatomy Project, an effort of six laboratories in five countries that adapts Human Connectome Project protocols to macaque and marmoset monkeys.
ocar.resolution: The project acquires high-resolution structural, functional, and diffusion MRI plus behavior from over 100 animals, quantitative tract-tracing with brain-wide counts of labeled neurons, and immunocytochemical cell-type maps to refine areal boundaries, then uses statistical modeling to compare tracer-based and MRI-based connectivity across individuals.
ocar.future_work: The authors aim to combine histology and imaging into improved cortical and subcortical atlases and to collect genetic and sociality-related behavioral data to ask how genetic variation shapes the connectome and behavior.

summaries.beginner: Brain scans used in people cannot be checked against the true wiring of the human brain. This project studies monkeys so researchers can compare those scans with gold-standard chemical labeling of actual connections.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 NeuroImage paper, Hayashi and colleagues introduce the NonHuman Primate Neuroimaging & Neuroanatomy Project, spanning six laboratories in five countries. They acquire Human Connectome Project–style structural, functional, and diffusion MRI in macaques and marmosets, together with quantitative tract-tracing and cell-type stains, in more than 100 animals. The goal is to test how well non-invasive connectivity measures match invasive ground truth and to build better areal atlases. Genetic and sociality-related behavioral data are collected in parallel.
summaries.advanced: This is a project description rather than a completed validation: the abstract reports acquisition plans and methods, not quantitative MRI–tracer agreement. Ground truth is still in macaque and marmoset, not human. “Over 100” animals is a combined macaque-plus-marmoset figure; species-specific sample sizes are not given. Catalog organism is tagged “other,” reflecting nonhuman primates rather than a registry volume.

plain_language_summary: Brain scans used in people cannot be checked against the true wiring of the human brain. This project studies monkeys so researchers can compare those scans with gold-standard chemical labeling of actual connections.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can resolve nanometer-scale structure in three dimensions, but the resulting datasets are huge and often noisy because imaging is sped up.
ocar.challenge: Advanced denoising methods exist, yet they are hard for most labs to use because of low-level programming, fussy parameter tuning, or slow computation.
ocar.action: Roels and colleagues introduce DenoisEM, an interactive, GPU-accelerated denoising plugin for ImageJ that uses parallel computing so users can tune parameters and process data quickly.
ocar.resolution: They report that DenoisEM is about one order of magnitude faster than related software and can accelerate data acquisition by a factor of 4 without significantly affecting data quality, while also helping visualization and (semi-)automated segmentation of ultrastructure in various volume EM datasets.
ocar.future_work: The work positions DenoisEM as a community tool for noisy 3D EM; broader uptake depends on applying it across more volume EM modalities and segmentation pipelines than the abstract names.

summaries.beginner: Three-dimensional electron-microscope pictures of cells are often grainy because the microscope is run quickly to save time. The authors made an easy computer tool that cleans up that grain so scientists can see and outline structures more clearly.
summaries.intermediate: Writing in Nature Communications in 2020, Roels and colleagues present DenoisEM, a GPU-accelerated ImageJ plugin for denoising electron microscopy. Large 3D EM volumes often take hours to days to acquire, and faster imaging adds noise that complicates automated analysis. The plugin is reported to be about ten times faster than related software and to allow roughly four-fold faster acquisition without a large drop in quality. Denoising also improved visualization and semi-automated segmentation of ultrastructure.
summaries.advanced: “One order of magnitude faster” and “a factor of 4” are the only speed claims in the abstract; datasets, noise models, and segmentation metrics are not specified here. The catalog tags volume EM at acquisition and segmentation stages. Benefits for segmentation are stated qualitatively (“benefits”), not as a benchmark table.

plain_language_summary: Three-dimensional electron-microscope pictures of cells are often grainy because the microscope is run quickly to save time. The authors made an easy computer tool that cleans up that grain so scientists can see and outline structures more clearly.

ocar.opportunity: To explain animal behavior one must identify, record from, and manipulate networks of connected neurons.
ocar.challenge: Genetic tools that label partners of a defined neuron in the reverse (postsynaptic-to-presynaptic) direction, with enough specificity for physiology, have been limited in Drosophila.
ocar.action: Cachero and colleagues engineered BAcTrace (Botulinum-Activated Tracer), a genetically encoded retrograde transsynaptic system based on botulinum neurotoxin A that travels between neurons and activates an otherwise silent transcription factor.
ocar.resolution: They validated BAcTrace at three connections in the fly olfactory system, showed that labeled partners can be recorded electrophysiologically, and in a highly divergent circuit correctly identified 12 of 16 connections previously seen by electron microscopy.
ocar.future_work: The authors present BAcTrace as a predominantly retrograde tracing tool for connectomic analyses in Drosophila, implying use in other circuits where EM or physiology is needed to confirm partners.

summaries.beginner: To understand a brain circuit, scientists need to see which cells talk to a chosen cell. This paper describes a genetic trick in fruit flies that labels those partner cells so they can be studied one by one.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2020), Cachero, Gkantia, Bates, Jefferis and colleagues introduce BAcTrace, a botulinum-toxin-based retrograde tracer for Drosophila. Engineered toxin moves from a starter neuron to connected partners and turns on a silent transcription factor. Validation in the olfactory system included three known connections, electrophysiological recordings from labeled cells, and recovery of 12 of 16 electron-microscopy-defined connections in a highly divergent circuit.
summaries.advanced: The tool is described as predominantly retrograde, not strictly exclusive. Success on 12 of 16 EM-defined connections in one challenging circuit leaves four false negatives; false-positive rates are not given in the abstract. Catalog method is electron microscopy because EM was used as a ground-truth check, not because BAcTrace itself is an EM method.

plain_language_summary: To understand a brain circuit, scientists need to see which cells talk to a chosen cell. This paper describes a genetic trick in fruit flies that labels those partner cells so they can be studied one by one.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila offers a workable balance of brain complexity and behavioral sophistication for studying how memories are encoded from molecules to circuits.
ocar.challenge: Even in this compact nervous system, linking genes, single neurons, physiology, and behavior into a coherent account of short-term olfactory associative learning remains unfinished.
ocar.action: Boto, Stahl, and Tomchik review how memories are encoded in the fly, emphasizing short-term memory, forward-genetic screens, reverse engineering of learning circuits, and functional imaging of plasticity loci.
ocar.resolution: They argue that numerical simplicity has allowed behavioral phenotypes to be ascribed in some cases to single neurons, that physiology has localized learning-related plasticity at major sites, and that emerging connectomes plus new tools are filling the anatomical roadmap for those studies.
ocar.future_work: The review frames these results as groundwork for deeper mechanistic understanding in the near future rather than as a closed account of memory encoding.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies can learn to link smells with reward or punishment, and their brains are small enough to study in detail. This review explains what is known about how that short-term learning is built into cells and circuits.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of neurogenetics (2020), Boto, Stahl, and Tomchik review cellular and circuit mechanisms of olfactory associative learning in Drosophila, with a focus on short-term memory. Forward-genetic screens have identified many necessary genes, some acting in single cells, while reverse engineering has mapped learning circuits with high precision. Functional imaging and physiology localize plasticity at major loci, and connectomics is expanding the anatomical map that those experiments use.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not new primary data; claims about single-neuron sufficiency and plasticity loci should be traced to the cited studies. The catalog tags fly and biological application, with no pipeline stage or named dataset. The abstract does not quantify genes, neurons, or effect sizes.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies can learn to link smells with reward or punishment, and their brains are small enough to study in detail. This review explains what is known about how that short-term learning is built into cells and circuits.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput electron microscopy such as FIB-SEM yields thousands of serial sections in which subcellular structure can be segmented and reconstructed in 3D.
ocar.challenge: Low contrast hinders segmentation, and current deep-learning methods still demand thousands of carefully curated manual labels that EM labs rarely have.
ocar.action: Khadangi, Boudier, and Rajagopal introduce EM-net, a scalable convolutional network for EM segmentation, and evaluate variants on two datasets, including a long-running public EM stack competition.
ocar.resolution: They report that EM-net variants outperform current deep-learning methods on small- and medium-sized ground-truth sets, and that an ensemble of top EM-net classifiers wins across a wide variety of evaluation metrics.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not specify next experiments; the implied use is training on limited labels in new FIB-SEM and related EM stacks.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of tiny cell parts are hard for computers to outline, and teaching the computer usually needs thousands of hand-drawn examples. The authors built a learning method that works well even when only a smaller set of those examples is available.
summaries.intermediate: In work listed here as bioRxiv 2020 (DOI pointing to ICPR 2021), Khadangi, Boudier, and Rajagopal present EM-net for segmenting electron microscopy, motivated by low-contrast FIB-SEM volumes. Manual annotation of thousands of ground-truth slices is a bottleneck. On two datasets, one from an EM stack competition running since 2012, EM-net variants beat existing deep-learning methods when ground truth is small or medium, and an ensemble of top base classifiers led on many metrics.
summaries.advanced: Exact scores, dataset names beyond the 2012 competition, and network architecture details are not in the abstract. “Small- and medium-sized” ground truth is not quantified here. Catalog stages span sectioning through infrastructure; method is tagged FIB-SEM. Treat ensemble superiority as a claim to inspect in the full paper’s tables.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of tiny cell parts are hard for computers to outline, and teaching the computer usually needs thousands of hand-drawn examples. The authors built a learning method that works well even when only a smaller set of those examples is available.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse counts in different brain regions are a basic ingredient of any whole-brain connectivity picture.
ocar.challenge: Volume electron microscopy can count synapses in 3D but cannot be applied brain-wide, while fluorescent puncta from synaptic proteins are easier to survey but are two-dimensional and not identical to synapses.
ocar.action: Santuy and colleagues genetically labeled MAGUK proteins PSD95 and SAP102, counted fluorescent puncta in hippocampal CA1 with spinning-disk confocal microscopy, and counted actual synapses in the same area with FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They derived a conversion ratio between FIB-SEM 3D synapse densities (synapses/µm³) and confocal 2D puncta densities (puncta/100 µm²), then applied it to existing confocal maps elsewhere. Estimated minimum synapse density was highest in isocortex, olfactory areas, hippocampal formation, and cortical subplate, lower in pallidum, hypothalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum, and variable in striatum and thalamus.
ocar.future_work: Because FIB-SEM cannot be run brain-wide, the conversion factor is offered as a way to estimate minimum synapse densities from confocal surveys in other regions.

summaries.beginner: Scientists want to know how many connection points exist in different parts of the brain. This study counted those points with a 3D electron microscope in one hippocampal area, then used that count as a ruler for quicker fluorescent pictures taken across the brain.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2020), Santuy, Merchán-Pérez and colleagues combined genetic labeling of PSD95 and SAP102 with spinning-disk confocal microscopy and FIB-SEM in hippocampal CA1. They converted 3D FIB-SEM synapse densities into a factor that rescales 2D puncta densities from other regions. Applying that factor, they report highest estimated densities in isocortex, olfactory areas, hippocampal formation, and cortical subplate, and low densities in pallidum, hypothalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum.
summaries.advanced: The conversion yields a minimum density estimate, not a full 3D census outside CA1. Only two MAGUKs (excitatory glutamatergic scaffolds) are labeled, so inhibitory synapses are outside the fluorescent tally. The abstract does not report the numeric ratio. Catalog methods are FIB-SEM and confocal; organism is untagged.

plain_language_summary: Scientists want to know how many connection points exist in different parts of the brain. This study counted those points with a 3D electron microscope in one hippocampal area, then used that count as a ruler for quicker fluorescent pictures taken across the brain.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans and P. pacificus occupy different habitats and behave differently, offering a pair of nematodes in which to ask how nervous systems diverge.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether evolutionary change sits in neuron number and targeting, in sensory endings, or in synaptic partner choice among processes that already occupy similar neighborhoods.
ocar.action: Hong, Hobert and colleagues assigned homologies for amphid neurons, first-layer interneurons, and several internal receptor neurons using soma position, axon projections, and dye uptake, then reconstructed a synaptic wiring diagram of amphid sensory neurons and interneurons in P. pacificus.
ocar.resolution: Neuron number and soma position are highly conserved, but several amphid cilia morphologies differ—most notably the absence of “winged” cilia in P. pacificus. Connectivity shows striking conservation and divergence relative to C. elegans, with little change in relative neighborhood of processes.
ocar.future_work: The authors’ impact statement locates the substrate of divergence in sensory perception and synaptic partner choice within invariant, prepatterned processes rather than in cell number or targeting.

summaries.beginner: Two roundworm species look similar at the level of individual nerve cells but live different lives. This study maps which cells connect in one species and compares that map with the famous wiring diagram of the other.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019; catalog year 2019), Hong, Riebesell, Bumbarger, Cook, Hobert and colleagues compare chemosensory neuroanatomy of Pristionchus pacificus with C. elegans. Homologies were assigned from position, projections, and dye filling. Cell number and somata are conserved, winged amphid cilia are missing in P. pacificus, and the amphid wiring diagram mixes conserved and diverged synapses despite stable process neighborhoods. The catalog links this to the C. elegans (White+) dataset.
summaries.advanced: The paper is a targeted amphid/interneuron reconstruction, not a whole-brain P. pacificus connectome. Homology assignments use multiple independent features but remain inferences. “Very little change in relative neighborhood” is qualitative. Catalog organism is elegans even though the new data are P. pacificus compared with C. elegans.

plain_language_summary: Two roundworm species look similar at the level of individual nerve cells but live different lives. This study maps which cells connect in one species and compares that map with the famous wiring diagram of the other.

ocar.opportunity: A single neuron and its synapses are the structural motif of the brain, but the gene-expression programs that specify each neuron type are poorly known.
ocar.challenge: Even in C. elegans, where anatomy and connectivity are defined at single-cell resolution, a molecular profile for most mature neuron classes was lacking.
ocar.action: Taylor, Hobert, Miller and colleagues produced single-cell transcriptomes for 52,412 neurons from the mature hermaphrodite nervous system.
ocar.resolution: The data resolve clusters matching 109 of the canonical 118 neuron classes (more than 90% of classes), reveal subtype splits often marked by neuropeptide-related genes, and are released at cengen.org with the SCeNGEA browser.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the catalog to help define mechanisms of lineage, anatomy, synaptic connectivity, and function for each C. elegans neuron type.

summaries.beginner: The roundworm’s nervous system is mapped cell by cell, but it was unclear which genes each cell type uses. This study read the gene activity of tens of thousands of individual worm neurons and matched them to known cell types.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Taylor and colleagues report single-cell RNA-seq of 52,412 C. elegans neurons, resolving 109 of 118 canonical hermaphrodite neuron classes. Subtypes often differ in neuropeptide-related genes. Data are public at cengen.org and through SCeNGEA. The work is catalogued with the White+ C. elegans dataset as a molecular companion to the anatomical connectome.
summaries.advanced: Nine canonical classes are not resolved here; “>90% of individual neuron classes” refers to class coverage, not every neuron in the animal. The preprint describes the mature hermaphrodite, not the male. Cluster-to-class assignments should be checked in the full resource. Catalog stage is graph_analysis even though the data are transcriptomic.

plain_language_summary: The roundworm’s nervous system is mapped cell by cell, but it was unclear which genes each cell type uses. This study read the gene activity of tens of thousands of individual worm neurons and matched them to known cell types.

ocar.opportunity: Cell-type-specific maps of who synapses onto whom are needed to constrain models of circuit function, including how inhibition is arranged on cortical pyramids.
ocar.challenge: Counting putative synapses across many neurons and compartments in intact tissue is slow if it depends on electron microscopy alone, and fluorescent synapse labels can alter physiology or lack multiplexed contrast.
ocar.action: Kuljis, Barth and colleagues built fluorogen-activating protein or YFP fused to a postsynaptic neuroligin-1 targeting sequence (FAP/YFPpost), expressed it sparsely with cytoplasmic dTomato via AAV in mouse somatosensory cortex, and aligned puncta with saturated Cre-dependent YFP in PV, SST, or VIP neurons.
ocar.resolution: FAPpost did not alter miniature EPSC or IPSC properties. Automated detection showed PV inputs as the predominant inhibitory source at soma and dendrites of layer 2/3 pyramids, concentrated on the primary apical dendrite, with SST inputs interleaved on higher-order branches.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose the reagents for large-scale, cell-type-specific quantitation of connectivity changes across development, learning, and disease.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells connect at tiny junctions that are hard to count under a regular microscope. The authors designed a glowing tag that sits at those junctions in mice so they can tally which inhibitory cell types contact which parts of a neuron.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2019), Kuljis and colleagues introduce FAP/YFPpost, a neuroligin-1–targeted fluorescent synapse label for mouse cortex. Sparse AAV expression with dTomato allowed compartment-specific puncta counts; far-red FAP emission enabled alignment with PV, SST, or VIP axons. On layer 2/3 pyramids, PV supplied most inhibitory appositions, especially on the primary apical dendrite, while SST contacts interleaved on secondary and higher-order branches. Miniature synaptic currents were unchanged by FAPpost.
summaries.advanced: Puncta-neurite apposition is putative connectivity, not EM-confirmed synapses. The abstract reports no change in mEPSCs/mIPSCs but does not list other physiological checks. VIP results are enabled by the labeling design but not quantified in the abstract. Catalog stage is alignment; organism is mouse.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells connect at tiny junctions that are hard to count under a regular microscope. The authors designed a glowing tag that sits at those junctions in mice so they can tally which inhibitory cell types contact which parts of a neuron.

ocar.opportunity: A complete, high-fidelity map of mammalian neurons and their physical connections would let researchers relate form to function and document structural disease, toward what the authors call a structural connectome.
ocar.challenge: Dense 3D image stacks still force much manual neuron identification because automatic tools struggle with packed cells in native tissue, introducing time cost and human bias.
ocar.action: Magliaro, Callara, Vanello, and Ahluwalia mini-review automatic and semi-automatic neuron segmentation algorithms and software, plus the metrics used to validate them, and briefly cover tissue clearing and new subcellular imaging methods.
ocar.resolution: They summarize strengths and limits of existing tools, note that clearing can improve optical access and stack quality, and argue that spines and thin neurites will demand new algorithms as imaging resolution increases.
ocar.future_work: The review points to processing tissues and images at subcellular scales as the next requirement for a more detailed structural map.

summaries.beginner: Turning microscope pictures of tangled brain cells into a wiring map still often means tracing by hand. This short review surveys computer programs that try to outline single neurons automatically and explains why that job is still hard.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology (2019), Magliaro and colleagues review tools for segmenting single neurons toward a structural connectome. They emphasize dense packing in 3D stacks, validation metrics, and the bias of manual tracing. Tissue clarification is noted as improving optical access. They argue that new methods imaging spines and thin neurites will require more robust algorithms. The catalog places the paper at the segmentation stage.
summaries.advanced: As a mini-review, it does not present a new benchmark winner or a single recommended pipeline. No quantitative comparison tables appear in the abstract. Catalog organism and method are empty; claims about mammalian whole-brain digitization are aspirational framing, not a completed reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Turning microscope pictures of tangled brain cells into a wiring map still often means tracing by hand. This short review surveys computer programs that try to outline single neurons automatically and explains why that job is still hard.

ocar.opportunity: Resting-state fMRI connectivity can define a robust brain-wide endophenotype in Fmr1-/y mice, a model of Fragile-X syndrome, raising the hope that the same macroscopic measure could track drug effects.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether functional connectivity is sensitive enough to detect pharmacological rescue, here via mGluR5 inhibition with AFQ056/Mavoglurant, which is assumed to normalize excitatory/inhibitory imbalance in FXS.
ocar.action: Zerbi, Wenderoth and colleagues combined rs-fMRI and diffusion-weighted imaging in Fmr1-/y mice treated with Mavoglurant, focusing on circuits related to social behavior.
ocar.resolution: Mutants showed impaired social interaction, reduced connectivity in three main functional networks, and altered network topology. At the group level, Mavoglurant rescued neither social behavior nor white-matter abnormalities, but restored functional connectivity in some, not all, of those circuits in a genotype-specific way.
ocar.future_work: The results imply that any behavioral benefit of Mavoglurant might be restricted to narrow functional domains, a hypothesis for more targeted assays than the abstract provides.

summaries.beginner: A mouse model of Fragile-X syndrome has unusual patterns of communication between brain regions. A drug partly normalized some of those brain-scan patterns but did not fix social behavior or white-matter structure in this study.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2019), Zerbi and colleagues tested whether rs-fMRI connectivity in Fmr1-/y mice responds to the mGluR5 inhibitor AFQ056/Mavoglurant. Mutants had social deficits, reduced connectivity in three main networks, and altered topology. Group-level Mavoglurant did not rescue social behavior or DWI white-matter abnormalities, yet had genotype-specific restoring effects on some functional circuits. The authors conclude rs-fMRI can detect system-level mGluR5 blockade.
summaries.advanced: Rescue is circuit-specific and dissociated from behavior and white matter at the group level; individual-level prediction is not claimed. The abstract does not name the three networks or give effect sizes. Catalog organism is untagged despite a mouse model. This is MRI connectivity, not synapse-level connectomics.

plain_language_summary: A mouse model of Fragile-X syndrome has unusual patterns of communication between brain regions. A drug partly normalized some of those brain-scan patterns but did not fix social behavior or white-matter structure in this study.

ocar.opportunity: Left–right brain asymmetry is a cardinal human trait, and decades of work have asked whether it is altered in psychiatric disorders and how it relates to age, sex, and other biological variables.
ocar.challenge: Prior findings were inconsistent and often underpowered, leaving even the healthy-population pattern of structural asymmetry incompletely mapped.
ocar.action: The ENIGMA-Laterality Working Group, in work summarized by Kong and colleagues, published six gray-matter morphological asymmetry studies over four years with total samples of roughly 3,500 to 17,000 individuals.
ocar.resolution: They mapped average asymmetry including a fronto-occipital cortical-thickness gradient, illustrated reproducibility across datasets, and related asymmetry to age, sex, handedness, and brain volume. Autism spectrum disorder was linked to subtly reduced thickness asymmetry at widespread cortical regions; pediatric OCD to altered subcortical asymmetry; major depressive disorder was not significantly associated with asymmetry changes.
ocar.future_work: Ongoing studies examine other disorders, and the consortium has laid groundwork for identifying shared genetic contributions to asymmetry and disease.

summaries.beginner: The left and right sides of the human brain are not mirror images, but small studies disagreed about how that imbalance relates to mental health. A huge international effort measured this leftover-right difference in thousands of people to get a clearer picture.
summaries.intermediate: In Human Brain Mapping (2019), Kong, Postema and the ENIGMA-Laterality group synthesize six gray-matter asymmetry studies with samples of about 3,500–17,000, one to two orders of magnitude larger than typical earlier work. They report a population-level cortical-thickness asymmetry gradient, test age, sex, handedness, and brain volume, and find subtle ASD-related thickness-asymmetry reduction, pediatric-OCD subcortical asymmetry changes, and no significant MDD association.
summaries.advanced: Effects for ASD are described as subtle and widespread; MDD’s null result is sample- and measure-specific to gray-matter morphological asymmetry. The abstract does not give effect sizes. This is macroscale MRI morphometry, not synaptic connectivity. Catalog axis is health_translation.

plain_language_summary: The left and right sides of the human brain are not mirror images, but small studies disagreed about how that imbalance relates to mental health. A huge international effort measured this leftover-right difference in thousands of people to get a clearer picture.

ocar.opportunity: Perfusing fixative through blood vessels is the gold-standard way, in animals, to preserve brain tissue for spatial molecular profiling, circuit tracing, and ultrastructural connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Human brain banks usually use immersion fixation, which is a barrier to architectural preservation, and the practicality and histological benefit of perfusion in human brains were not well defined.
ocar.action: McFadden, McKenzie and colleagues systematically reviewed four databases (protocol preregistered) and found 35 studies reporting perfusion fixation of 558 human brains, extracting methods and any comparisons with immersion.
ocar.resolution: Approaches varied widely (in situ vs ex situ, vessels, washout, fixative, pressure, postfixation). Qualitative synthesis gave moderate-confidence evidence that perfusion yields equal or better subjective histology than immersion for relatively large tissue volumes in equal or shorter time.
ocar.future_work: They recommend comparing in situ versus ex situ perfusion, testing washout solutions, and defining which donors benefit most relative to immersion.

summaries.beginner: Animal brains used for fine wiring maps are usually preserved by pumping chemicals through blood vessels, but donated human brains are typically soaked instead. This review gathers every study that tried the pumping method in people and asks whether it really preserves tissue better.
summaries.intermediate: In Acta Neuropathologica Communications (2019), McFadden and colleagues screened 4,489 abstracts and 214 full texts, including 35 studies (558 human brains). Perfusion methods were heterogeneous. Compared with immersion, perfusion produced equal or greater subjective histology quality for relatively large volumes in equal or less time (moderate-confidence synthesis). The paper is offered as a methods resource for human and large-animal brain banking.
summaries.advanced: Evidence quality is “moderate confidence” and outcomes are subjective histology, not EM-traceable connectomes. Heterogeneity of protocols limits meta-analytic pooling; the abstract does not identify a single best recipe. Catalog stages include preparation, proofreading, and infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Animal brains used for fine wiring maps are usually preserved by pumping chemicals through blood vessels, but donated human brains are typically soaked instead. This review gathers every study that tried the pumping method in people and asks whether it really preserves tissue better.

ocar.opportunity: Melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) send axons to multiple brain regions that control circadian and pupil functions, so their terminal ultrastructure is a window on long-range retinal circuits.
ocar.challenge: Seeing both the whole neuron and its synapses in many targets requires a label that works for correlated light and electron microscopy (CLEM) without losing distant terminals.
ocar.action: Kim, Ellisman, Hattar and colleagues used a membrane-targeted genetic CLEM probe to reconstruct ipRGC form and synaptic fine structure in several retinorecipient areas, including SCN, OPN, and lateral geniculate subregions.
ocar.resolution: Despite ipRGCs being the only direct retinal input to OPN and SCN, terminal arbors and boutons differed markedly by target. In SCN they also found a network of dendro-dendritic chemical synapses, with ipRGC axons preferring those linked cells.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the methods as a template for other CLEM studies of long-distance circuits at high resolution.

summaries.beginner: Some eye cells that sense light send messages to many places in the brain, not just the seeing centers. This study tagged those cells so they could be followed with both ordinary and electron microscopes all the way to their endings.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell Reports (2019), Kim and colleagues apply a membrane-targeted CLEM label to mouse ipRGCs (catalog dataset DS09/DS10 mouse retina). Terminal architecture differed across SCN, OPN, and LGN subregions even though OPN and SCN receive only this direct retinal input. SCN contained dendro-dendritic chemical synapses that preferentially received ipRGC synapses. Methods are offered for other long-range CLEM projects.
summaries.advanced: “Only direct retinal input” to OPN and SCN is a stated premise, not re-proven here. Quantitative bouton morphometrics are not in the abstract. Catalog methods are CLEM and electron microscopy; organism is mouse.

plain_language_summary: Some eye cells that sense light send messages to many places in the brain, not just the seeing centers. This study tagged those cells so they could be followed with both ordinary and electron microscopes all the way to their endings.

ocar.opportunity: A neocortical area typically receives from and projects to dozens of others, so the brain must route information to the right pathway at the right time—what the authors call pathway gating.
ocar.challenge: How a region that hears both visual and auditory streams, for example, can gate one in and the other out is not settled, and competing gating mechanisms exist.
ocar.action: Wang and Yang review experimental and computational evidence for a disinhibitory circuit motif as a mechanism of flexible pathway gating, and note its increasing prevalence from sensory to association cortex.
ocar.resolution: They marshal support that disinhibition can implement pathway input gating, briefly compare alternative or complementary mechanisms, and collect predictions and open questions.
ocar.future_work: The review closes by listing predictions and open questions for how this motif operates in the complex brain.

summaries.beginner: Your brain must choose which incoming signals to pay attention to, like reading in a noisy café. This review discusses a wiring pattern in which taking the brakes off some cells can open one information route while closing another.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2018), Xiao-Jing Wang and Guangyu Yang review a disinhibitory motif as a candidate for flexible pathway gating in mammalian neocortex. They argue the motif becomes more prominent toward association areas and compare it with other gating ideas. The piece is catalogued under graph analysis as a conceptual circuit paper, not a new connectome.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review: no new experiments or quantified motif frequencies appear in the abstract. “Increasing preponderance” from sensory to association cortex is cited as recent work, not measured here. Alternative gating mechanisms are acknowledged as complementary rather than ruled out.

plain_language_summary: Your brain must choose which incoming signals to pay attention to, like reading in a noisy café. This review discusses a wiring pattern in which taking the brakes off some cells can open one information route while closing another.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal prostheses try to restore partial vision after degenerative disease by electrically stimulating remaining neurons, so stimulus waveforms need a realistic tissue-and-circuit model.
ocar.challenge: Degeneration includes early cell death and anatomical change plus altered firing that may interfere with prosthetic control, and those states are hard to explore exhaustively in vitro.
ocar.action: Loizos, Lazzi and colleagues combined a connectome-based neural network (accurate morphology and synapses) with an admittance model of bulk tissue and electronics, then computationally degenerated mouse retina including DS09/DS10-tagged circuitry.
ocar.resolution: ON ganglion-cell stimulation thresholds did not notably change in beginning degeneration. They propose an asymmetric biphasic current waveform to subdue spontaneous firing and increase control of ganglion-cell spike patterns.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the asymmetric waveform as a candidate for better prosthetic control; in vivo tests are not reported here.

summaries.beginner: When the light-sensing layer of the eye dies, doctors try to send electrical pulses to the remaining cells to restore some sight. This computer model of a damaged retina tests which pulse shapes might steer those cells more reliably.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering (2018), Loizos and colleagues model electrical stimulation of healthy versus early-degenerated retina using a connectome-based network plus tissue electronics. ON ganglion-cell thresholds were largely unchanged at beginning degeneration. An asymmetric biphasic waveform is proposed to quiet spontaneous firing and improve control. The catalog tags DS09/DS10 mouse retina and infrastructure/modeling stages.
summaries.advanced: Results are from a computational degeneration, not from implanted patients. Only beginning-stage degeneration and ON ganglion cells are highlighted. “Did not notably vary” is qualitative. Waveform benefit is shown in simulation of the proposed currents.

plain_language_summary: When the light-sensing layer of the eye dies, doctors try to send electrical pulses to the remaining cells to restore some sight. This computer model of a damaged retina tests which pulse shapes might steer those cells more reliably.

ocar.opportunity: With connectomes now in hand for both the C. elegans hermaphrodite and adult male, sexual dimorphism of a whole nervous system can be described comprehensively.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear how sex-specific neurons integrate with shared circuitry and how much dimorphism hides inside neurons present in both sexes.
ocar.action: Emmons reviews the male and hermaphrodite connectomes and the circuits for sex-specific behaviors and shared navigational choices that optimize reproduction.
ocar.resolution: The nervous system has 294 shared neurons, plus 8 hermaphrodite-specific and 91 male-specific cells, and in the male 16% of input to the shared component comes from male-specific neurons. Sex-specific cells mainly, but not only, control egg-laying or copulation and act with shared neurons in navigation, while substantial dimorphism, including synaptic connectivity, exists inside the shared component itself.
ocar.future_work: The review presents these maps as opening identification and study of the circuits that underlie sexual behaviors.

summaries.beginner: Male and female roundworms share many of the same nerve cells but use their brains differently for mating and egg-laying. This review explains how extra male cells plug into the shared wiring and how even shared cells connect differently in each sex.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2018), S. W. Emmons synthesizes the C. elegans male connectome with the hermaphrodite map (catalog dataset DS01). Shared neurons number 294; sex-unique neurons are 8 (hermaphrodite) and 91 (male), and male-specific cells provide 16% of input onto the shared network. Dimorphism includes connectivity among sex-shared neurons, not only the unique cells.
summaries.advanced: Percentages and cell counts are from the reviewed connectomes; this article is not itself a new reconstruction. “Primarily but not exclusively” sex-unique behavioral roles caution against a strict one-function mapping. Catalog method is empty; organism is elegans.

plain_language_summary: Male and female roundworms share many of the same nerve cells but use their brains differently for mating and egg-laying. This review explains how extra male cells plug into the shared wiring and how even shared cells connect differently in each sex.

ocar.opportunity: Visual motion on the retina drives a cohort of ganglion cells whose population activity encodes multiple information streams extracted by parallel circuits.
ocar.challenge: How those streams are built, especially direction selectivity, requires integrating function, connectivity, and models at a level of detail that keeps changing.
ocar.action: Wei reviews neural mechanisms of motion processing in the mammalian retina, focusing on the direction-selective circuit as studied with functional, connectomic, and modeling methods, and also covering other motion features in broader RGC populations.
ocar.resolution: The review emphasizes that motion detection remains robust because multiple mechanisms are engaged dynamically and in a stimulus-dependent way at both single-cell and population levels.
ocar.future_work: Open directions are those implied by remaining puzzles in how broader RGC populations encode motion features beyond classical direction selectivity.

summaries.beginner: Your eye’s inner wiring can tell which way something is moving even before the rest of the brain weighs in. This review explains how mouse and other mammalian retinas build that motion sense from specific cell types and their connections.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Vision Science (2018), Wei Wei surveys motion processing in the mammalian retina, with the direction-selective circuit as the best-worked example spanning physiology, connectomics, and models. Other motion features in broader ganglion-cell populations are included. A central theme is stimulus-dependent recruitment of multiple mechanisms. The catalog tags DS09/DS10 mouse retina.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new EM volume. “Unprecedented detail” refers to the cited literature. No new counts of cell types or synapses appear in the abstract. Catalog organism is mouse; the title says mammalian retina more broadly.

plain_language_summary: Your eye’s inner wiring can tell which way something is moving even before the rest of the brain weighs in. This review explains how mouse and other mammalian retinas build that motion sense from specific cell types and their connections.

ocar.opportunity: In sensory cortex, nearby neurons encode different stimulus attributes and send them to different long-range targets, so local wiring rules must reconcile response similarity with projection identity.
ocar.challenge: Whether neurons that project to different higher visual areas connect to each other locally, or form segregated subnetworks, was unclear in mouse primary visual cortex.
ocar.action: Kim, Znamenskiy, Iacaruso, and Mrsic-Flogel recorded local connectivity and visual responses of layer 2/3 neurons in mouse V1 that project to anterolateral (AL) versus posteromedial (PM) higher visual areas.
ocar.resolution: Although visual response properties of AL- and PM-projecting cells were often similar, they avoided connecting with each other. Projection target, in addition to response similarity, therefore constrains local synapses. The authors propose that reduced crosstalk lets these output channels function independently.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not outline further experiments; the implied question is how general this segregation is across other cortical projection pairs.

summaries.beginner: Neighboring brain cells that send messages to different destinations might still talk to each other locally. In mouse visual cortex, cells aimed at two different next-stage areas actually avoided connecting, even when they liked similar pictures.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2018), Mean-Hwan Kim and colleagues compare layer 2/3 V1 neurons projecting to mouse higher visual areas AL versus PM. Response properties often overlapped, but the two projection classes avoided reciprocal local connections. The paper argues that projection target is a wiring rule beyond feature similarity, supporting independent output channels.
summaries.advanced: “Often similar” responses and “avoided making connections” are qualitative in the abstract; connection probabilities are not given here. Only AL and PM, and layer 2/3, are tested. Catalog stage is synapses; organism is untagged in the catalog despite mouse V1.

plain_language_summary: Neighboring brain cells that send messages to different destinations might still talk to each other locally. In mouse visual cortex, cells aimed at two different next-stage areas actually avoided connecting, even when they liked similar pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding a microcircuit’s computation requires both a complete synaptic map and a grasp of the information-processing tasks it performs—in this case, distributing scotopic rod signals into ON and OFF cone pathways.
ocar.challenge: How the AII amacrine cell filters and routes distinct components of rod bipolar input to downstream cone bipolar cells, and whether connectivity is unbiased across OFF cone bipolar subtypes, was not fully specified.
ocar.action: Graydon, Briggman, Singer, Diamond and colleagues combined serial block-face EM reconstructions with paired whole-cell recordings in mouse retina.
ocar.resolution: SBEM showed AIIs preferentially connect to OFF cone bipolar subtype CBC2. Depending on network activation, AIIs transmit distinct components of single rod-bipolar synaptic input to ON and OFF cone bipolars.
ocar.future_work: The findings highlight synaptic and circuit features that let intermediate neurons filter information; extending the same combined EM-physiology approach to other AII targets is implied rather than stated.

summaries.beginner: In dim light, signals from rod cells must be handed off into pathways that say “lights up” or “lights down.” This study mapped the tiny connections of a go-between cell in the mouse retina and listened to those connections electrically.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2018), Graydon and colleagues dissect the mouse AII amacrine microcircuit that distributes rod-bipolar information to ON and OFF cone bipolar cells. SBEM reconstructions (catalog DS09/DS10, method SBF-SEM) show preferential AII contacts onto CBC2. Paired recordings show that what the AII passes on from a single rod bipolar depends on network activation.
summaries.advanced: Preference for CBC2 is a reconstruction result; other OFF CBC subtypes are not quantified in the abstract. Physiology depends on “level of network activation,” so transfer is state-dependent rather than a single linear filter. Catalog stage is sectioning.

plain_language_summary: In dim light, signals from rod cells must be handed off into pathways that say “lights up” or “lights down.” This study mapped the tiny connections of a go-between cell in the mouse retina and listened to those connections electrically.

ocar.opportunity: A refined parcellation of mouse cortical areas makes it possible to ask how inter-areal wiring is organized as a weighted graph, in analogy to macaque cortex.
ocar.challenge: Earlier mouse studies disagreed on consistency, density, and graph statistics of the cortical connectome.
ocar.action: Gămănuţ, Kennedy, Burkhalter and colleagues made 27 retrograde tracer injections in 19 areas of a 47-area mouse neocortex parcellation, then counted labeled neurons on flat mounts with multiple histological markers.
ocar.resolution: Connection weights to each area are lognormally distributed over five orders of magnitude, yielding a distinct connectivity profile per area, as in macaque, and network density is 97% versus 66% reported in macaque. Weighted-graph analysis shows similar global efficiency but weaker spatial clustering than macaque, and these features differ significantly from earlier mouse reports.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames the dataset as correcting prior mouse estimates; further comparison across species and parcellations is implicit.

summaries.beginner: Researchers injected tracers into many regions of the mouse’s outer brain to see who talks to whom. They found an extremely dense web of connections, with each region having its own characteristic mix of strong and weak links.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2018), Gămănuţ and colleagues report 27 retrograde injections covering 19 of 47 mouse neocortical areas. Weights spanning five lognormal orders of magnitude define area-specific profiles. They estimate 97% connection density (versus 66% in macaque), similar global efficiency, and weaker spatial clustering than macaque, diverging from earlier mouse connectomes.
summaries.advanced: Density is among injected/parcellated areas, not every possible pair in an unparcellated sheet. Nineteen of 47 areas were injection targets; uninjected areas contribute as sources of labeled cells. “Five orders of magnitude” and 97%/66% are the quantitative claims to verify in figures. Catalog organism is mouse; method is empty (tracer study).

plain_language_summary: Researchers injected tracers into many regions of the mouse’s outer brain to see who talks to whom. They found an extremely dense web of connections, with each region having its own characteristic mix of strong and weak links.

ocar.opportunity: Large datasets now describe cortical composition and properties, creating a chance to simulate in-vivo-like circuit activity instead of only cataloguing parts.
ocar.challenge: Quantitative modeling of cortex under realistic conditions remains difficult, and it is unclear which biological details are required to match visual physiology.
ocar.action: Arkhipov, Gouwens and colleagues built and publicly released a biophysically detailed 45,000-neuron model of mouse V1 layer 4 receiving thalamo-cortical visual input (catalog DS12 L4 barrel cortex / visual L4), ran a battery of visual stimuli, and compared with published and new in vivo experiments, including optogenetic perturbations.
ocar.resolution: Simulations reproduced many observations. Rules of functional synaptic connectivity were critical to in silico versus in vivo agreement. Extreme simplification still performed satisfactorily on many measures, though quantitative agreement suffered.
ocar.future_work: They present the model, code, and results as enabling a next generation of data-driven in vivo models of activity and computation.

summaries.beginner: Scientists built a detailed computer version of one layer of mouse visual cortex, with tens of thousands of cells, and showed it movies. The fake circuit behaved much like a real one, especially when the wiring followed rules about who likes the same pictures.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2018), Arkhipov and Allen Institute colleagues report a 45,000-neuron biophysical model of mouse V1 layer 4. A visual-stimulus battery, compared with in vivo data including optogenetic perturbations, matched many phenomena when functional connectivity rules were included. Simplified neurons still captured many measures but with worse quantitative fit. Code and model are public.
summaries.advanced: Catalog dataset is DS12 L4 barrel cortex while the abstract specifies primary visual cortex layer 4—treat the registry tag as catalog metadata, not a claim that this is barrel cortex. “Many” reproduced observations are unnamed in the abstract. Simplification “deficiencies” are asserted without listing which metrics broke.

plain_language_summary: Scientists built a detailed computer version of one layer of mouse visual cortex, with tens of thousands of cells, and showed it movies. The fake circuit behaved much like a real one, especially when the wiring followed rules about who likes the same pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Several neurodegenerative diseases appear to spread pathogenic proteins along brain circuits, producing stereotyped regional topography; network diffusion models (NDM) have been applied to Alzheimer’s and frontotemporal dementia.
ocar.challenge: Whether NDM applies to progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a synucleinopathy/tauopathy with stereotyped striatal-then-cortical atrophy, and whether direction of spread matters, was unknown.
ocar.action: Pandya, Mezias, and Raj fit directional and non-directional connectome-based NDM to empirical PSP topography.
ocar.resolution: PSP was amenable to NDM as previously used in AD and FTD. Using a directional human connectome significantly improved fit versus a non-directional one; both anterograde (soma to terminal) and retrograde modes explained PSP topography better than undirected transmission.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue these results should influence future studies of trans-neuronal transmission and directed connectome models of disease spread.

summaries.beginner: Some brain diseases seem to creep from region to region along the brain’s wiring. This study asks whether a rare parkinsonian disorder follows those wires, and whether the direction of the wires matters.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neurology (2017), Pandya, Mezias, and Raj apply a network diffusion model to progressive supranuclear palsy. PSP fit connectome-based spread similarly to prior AD/FTD work. Directional connectomes outperformed undirected ones, with both anterograde and retrograde modes beating non-directional transmission. They conclude structural-network architecture mediates PSP spread, likely via trans-neuronal transmission.
summaries.advanced: This is modeling of empirical atrophy/pathology topography, not new histopathology. The abstract does not report numeric fit statistics. Hallmark proteins (tau versus synuclein) are discussed in the disease framing; the model itself is network diffusion on a human connectome. Catalog stage is graph_analysis.

plain_language_summary: Some brain diseases seem to creep from region to region along the brain’s wiring. This study asks whether a rare parkinsonian disorder follows those wires, and whether the direction of the wires matters.

ocar.opportunity: Hippocampal CA3 is classically treated as a homogeneous autoassociative net for pattern completion, yet spatial encoding and memory already look heterogeneous along the proximodistal (transverse) axis.
ocar.challenge: Whether intrinsic properties, long-range inputs, recurrent excitation, and memory-trace reactivation also form proximodistal gradients was unclear.
ocar.action: Sun, Siegelbaum and colleagues measured intrinsic membrane properties, mossy-fiber versus entorhinal synaptic strengths, and fear-memory reactivation along dorsal CA3 in mouse.
ocar.resolution: Mossy-fiber strength decreases, and direct entorhinal excitation increases, along the proximodistal axis. Fear-memory reactivation was nonuniform and most robust in mid-CA3 (CA3b), the region of strongest net recurrent excitation.
ocar.future_work: They suggest these gradients may explain distinct spatial encoding and behavioral roles of CA3 subregions.

summaries.beginner: A seahorse-shaped brain area used for memory was long treated as one uniform network. This mouse study shows that different strips of that area have different electrical personalities and replay fear memories to different degrees.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2017), Sun and colleagues report proximodistal gradients in dorsal mouse CA3. Mossy-fiber synaptic strength falls and entorhinal excitation rises from proximal to distal CA3. Fear-memory traces reactivated most robustly in CA3b, where net recurrent excitation was strongest. Heterogeneity in intrinsic properties and connectivity may underlie known functional differences along this axis.
summaries.advanced: “Striking” gradients and “most robust” reactivation are not quantified in the abstract. The classical autoassociative view is revised, not discarded. Catalog axis is biological_application; organism is mouse. Only dorsal CA3 is described.

plain_language_summary: A seahorse-shaped brain area used for memory was long treated as one uniform network. This mouse study shows that different strips of that area have different electrical personalities and replay fear memories to different degrees.

ocar.opportunity: In physical networks, behavior such as synchronization depends on hard-wired topology; control theory can relate that architecture to how much energy is needed to steer the system.
ocar.challenge: Closed-form links between specific classes of edges (driver to non-driver) and minimum control energy, and what that means for brains, were lacking.
ocar.action: Kim, Bassett and colleagues derive such expressions from linear network control theory and apply them to high-resolution connectomes from Drosophila, mouse, and human.
ocar.resolution: The mathematics relates control energy to driver–non-driver links. Applied to brains, they suggest an advantage for the human brain in supporting diverse dynamics at small energetic cost while remaining robust, and they illustrate clinically accessible manipulation by removing single edges.
ocar.future_work: They argue the results should inspire new network analysis and distributed-control design, including targeted edge manipulation.

summaries.beginner: Steering a network of connected parts takes energy, and that energy depends on how the parts are wired. The authors work out that relationship and then look at wiring maps from fly, mouse, and human brains.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Physics (2017), Jason Z. Kim, Danielle Bassett and colleagues use linear control theory to relate minimum control energy to connections from driver to non-driver nodes. They apply the theory to Drosophila, mouse, and human connectomes. They suggest human brain architecture supports diverse dynamics cheaply and robustly, and they simulate control-performance changes after single-edge removal.
summaries.advanced: Results are linear control-theoretic, not measured metabolic costs. “Clinically accessible targeted manipulation” is a modeling illustration (single-edge removal), not a therapy. Catalog organism is fly despite multi-species application. Connectome spatial scale (EM versus MRI) is not specified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Steering a network of connected parts takes energy, and that energy depends on how the parts are wired. The authors work out that relationship and then look at wiring maps from fly, mouse, and human brains.

ocar.opportunity: Animal connectomes let researchers test how anatomical structure shapes resting functional connectivity in a mammalian cortex smaller than human or macaque.
ocar.challenge: Relating directed tracing-based weights to fMRI correlations, community structure, and simulated dynamics requires carefully curated anatomy plus comparable functional data.
ocar.action: Díaz-Parra, Sporns and colleagues combined a directed rat cortical network from meta-analysis of tracing with resting-state fMRI from 14 anesthetized Wistar rats, and ran neural-mass simulations on the empirical connectome.
ocar.resolution: Functional connection strength tracked anatomical weights (maximum Spearman correlation reported but not numerically readable in this abstract). Same-community regions formed more mutual weighted connections; functional communities were enriched for dense anatomical motifs beyond lower-order topology. Simulations of the rat connectome correlated with measured functional connectivity (maximum Pearson correlation likewise not numerically given here).
ocar.future_work: Highlights emphasize that densely connected motifs and connectome topology help generate realistic resting dynamics, motivating further structure–function tests.

summaries.beginner: This study compared a wiring map of the rat cortex, built from many tracer studies, with brain scans of resting rats. Places that are more strongly wired also tended to pulse together, and a computer model using the wiring map could reproduce much of that pulsing.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2017), Díaz-Parra, Canals, Moratal, Sporns and colleagues compare a directed rat cortical connectome with rs-fMRI in 14 anesthetized Wistar rats. BOLD correlations followed anatomical weights; functional communities were enriched in dense anatomical motifs not explained by simpler graph features. Neural-mass simulations on the empirical connectome produced realistic functional connectivity. Catalog organism is “other” (rat).
summaries.advanced: Exact Spearman and Pearson maxima are missing from this abstract extract (typesetting placeholders). Anesthesia and n=14 limit generality. Motif enrichment is claimed after controlling for lower-order topology, a key caveat to inspect in the paper. Catalog stages include proofreading, graph_analysis, and modeling.

plain_language_summary: This study compared a wiring map of the rat cortex, built from many tracer studies, with brain scans of resting rats. Places that are more strongly wired also tended to pulse together, and a computer model using the wiring map could reproduce much of that pulsing.

ocar.opportunity: A synapse-resolution connectome is the wiring diagram needed to understand a circuit, but imaging-based reconstruction is slow, labor-intensive, and expensive.
ocar.challenge: High-throughput DNA sequencing is fast and cheap, yet converting synaptic partners into sequenceable DNA had not been achieved.
ocar.action: Peikon, Kebschull, Zador and colleagues present SYNseq: unique RNA barcodes in each neuron are targeted to synapses, pre- and postsynaptic barcodes are crosslinked across the cleft, extracted, and joined for sequencing.
ocar.resolution: The molecular scheme is demonstrated, but in their hands inefficiency of barcode joining precluded widespread application at the time of writing.
ocar.future_work: They expect further development to enable high-speed, low-cost tracing of complex circuits.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every connection in a brain with microscopes is slow and costly. This paper tries to turn those connections into DNA barcodes that a sequencer could read, but the joining step was still too inefficient for routine use.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2017), Peikon, Zador and colleagues introduce SYNseq, which labels neurons with RNA barcodes, localizes them to synapses, crosslinks pre- and postsynaptic barcodes, and concatenates them for sequencing. The method in principle yields a connectome as a list of barcode pairs. They frankly report that barcode-joining inefficiency blocked wide application. Catalog stages are proofreading and graph_analysis.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint whose central negative result is joining inefficiency; no circuit reconstruction is claimed. Organism is not specified in the catalog or abstract. Treat SYNseq as a proof of concept, not a deployed alternative to EM.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every connection in a brain with microscopes is slow and costly. This paper tries to turn those connections into DNA barcodes that a sequencer could read, but the joining step was still too inefficient for routine use.

ocar.opportunity: A formal link between neural network structure and emergent function would explain how brains process information.
ocar.challenge: Standard graph descriptions that ignore the direction of synaptic transmission miss the topology that actually guides information flow.
ocar.action: Reimann, Markram, Hess and colleagues built directed graphs of a neocortical local network and analyzed them with algebraic topology, tracking how activity binds neurons into cliques and cavities.
ocar.resolution: They report an intricate topology of neuronal cliques bound into cavities that guide correlated activity. Stimuli bind synaptically connected neurons into functional cliques and cavities that evolve stereotypically toward peak complexity. They propose that the brain processes stimuli by forming increasingly complex functional cliques and cavities.
ocar.future_work: The proposal that this sequence is a processing mechanism is a hypothesis for other areas and stimuli beyond the local neocortical network studied.

summaries.beginner: This paper treats brain wiring as one-way streets and uses a branch of mathematics that studies holes and clusters. The authors suggest that as a stimulus is processed, groups of cells form more and more complex shapes in that mathematical space.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2016), Reimann, Nolte, Markram, Hess and colleagues apply algebraic topology to directed synaptic graphs of a local neocortical network. They describe abundant cliques bound into cavities that relate to correlated activity. Stimulus-evoked activity is said to evolve through a stereotyped sequence of increasing complexity. The catalog tags graph_analysis.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the species, area, or whether the network is biological or a reconstructed/model microcircuit (Blue Brain-style). Clique/cavity counts and statistics are not given here. Causal language (“guide,” “processes stimuli by”) is interpretive.

plain_language_summary: This paper treats brain wiring as one-way streets and uses a branch of mathematics that studies holes and clusters. The authors suggest that as a stimulus is processed, groups of cells form more and more complex shapes in that mathematical space.

ocar.opportunity: Community detection—finding groups of nodes that connect more among themselves than with others—is central to modern network science, including brain graphs.
ocar.challenge: The problem is ill-defined: there is no universal definition of community, nor agreed protocols for validation and algorithm comparison, generating confusion that slows the field.
ocar.action: Fortunato and Hric offer a user guide through the main aspects of community detection, pointing out strengths and weaknesses of popular methods and giving practical directions.
ocar.resolution: The review organizes definitions, methods, and misconceptions rather than introducing a single new algorithm.
ocar.future_work: They aim to reduce confusion so that subsequent method development and applications rest on clearer protocols.

summaries.beginner: People often want to find clusters in a network, like groups of friends who mostly talk among themselves. This guide explains why that task is surprisingly slippery and how to use common clustering methods without being misled.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2016 review (catalog venue arXiv.org; related to Physics Reports), Fortunato and Hric survey community detection. They stress that communities lack a unique definition and that validation and benchmarking are unsettled. The piece is a methods guide for network science, catalogued as a graph-analysis bridge paper without a specific organism or dataset.
summaries.advanced: No new algorithm or brain-specific benchmark is claimed. Users still must choose a community definition; the guide cannot make the problem well-posed. Catalog axis is bridge.

plain_language_summary: People often want to find clusters in a network, like groups of friends who mostly talk among themselves. This guide explains why that task is surprisingly slippery and how to use common clustering methods without being misled.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing hermaphrodite and male C. elegans connectomes revealed sexually dimorphic synapses among neurons present in both sexes, raising the question of how shared neurons acquire sex-specific wiring.
ocar.challenge: Whether those dimorphic connections arise by sex-specific formation, pruning, or both, and whether sexual identity of pre- or postsynaptic cells is sufficient to switch the pattern, was unknown.
ocar.action: Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert analyzed sex-specific functions of shared neurons and the developmental trajectory of their synapses, including genetic reversal of sexual identity in individual cells.
ocar.resolution: Many neurons first form hybrid male-plus-hermaphrodite synapses, then prune in a sex-specific way. Changing the sexual identity of either the pre- or the postsynaptic neuron alone converts connectivity to the opposite-sex pattern. A dimorphically expressed, conserved transcription factor is necessary and sufficient for sex-specific connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The authors present these results as new insight into sex-specific circuit development, a framework for other sexually dimorphic synapses.

summaries.beginner: Male and female roundworms share many of the same nerve cells, yet those cells end up wired differently. This study shows that extra connections are built in both sexes and then trimmed away according to the animal’s sex.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2016), Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert show that sex-shared C. elegans neurons initially form hybrid synaptic patterns that are later pruned sex-specifically (catalog DS01). Reversing sexual identity in either partner rewires the pair to the opposite-sex pattern. A conserved, dimorphically expressed transcription factor is necessary and sufficient for those connectivity patterns.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the transcription factor or count how many connections were scored. “Many neurons” is not a complete census of dimorphic synapses. Necessity and sufficiency are genetic claims to inspect in the figures. Catalog organism is elegans.

plain_language_summary: Male and female roundworms share many of the same nerve cells, yet those cells end up wired differently. This study shows that extra connections are built in both sexes and then trimmed away according to the animal’s sex.

ocar.opportunity: Chimera states—coexistence of coherent and incoherent activity—have been analyzed in complex networks but not extensively in modular architectures like a community-structured nervous system.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether mixed electrical coupling within communities and chemical coupling across them can produce chimera-like dynamics in a connectome-inspired network.
ocar.action: Hizanidis and colleagues simulated a network inspired by the C. elegans connectome, organized into six communities of chaotic bursting neurons, with electrical synapses within and chemical synapses between communities, and compared networks sharing features of that connectome.
ocar.resolution: The two coupling types produced chimera-like states: larger communities more synchronized, smaller ones desynchronized. They quantified this with the Kuramoto order parameter plus chimera-like and metastability indices. Similar results in related modular networks suggest the phenomenon can be generic under their assumptions.
ocar.future_work: They suggest such states might provide insight into more complex modular brains if the same coupling assumptions hold.

summaries.beginner: Some networks can have one group of parts moving in lockstep while another group is out of step. Using a computer model inspired by a worm’s brain, the authors show that this split can appear when cells inside a group are wired differently from cells between groups.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2015), Hizanidis and colleagues model chimera-like states on a six-community network inspired by the C. elegans connectome (catalog DS01). Intra-community electrical and inter-community chemical synapses yielded partial synchrony concentrated in larger communities. They report Kuramoto, chimera-like, and metastability indices, and find similar behavior in networks that share C. elegans-like features.
summaries.advanced: This is a numerical study of bursting oscillators, not recorded worm activity. “Inspired by” the connectome is not a claim of biophysical completeness. Generality is limited to their coupling assumptions. Catalog stage is modeling; organism is elegans.

plain_language_summary: Some networks can have one group of parts moving in lockstep while another group is out of step. Using a computer model inspired by a worm’s brain, the authors show that this split can appear when cells inside a group are wired differently from cells between groups.

ocar.opportunity: Human macroconnectomics increasingly treats the number of reconstructed diffusion streamlines (NOS) as a measure of cortico-cortical connection strength.
ocar.challenge: How NOS relates to gold-standard tract-tracing measures of projection strength was poorly understood.
ocar.action: Van den Heuvel and colleagues compared DWI-derived NOS and fiber density from 10 rhesus macaques with tracing-based strengths from CoCoMac and the high-resolution Markov–Kennedy macaque dataset.
ocar.resolution: NOS and reconstructed-fiber density positively correlated with tracing-based connectivity strength in both tracing resources (both P < 0.001). They conclude that in vivo DWI connectomes can represent fairly realistic estimates of white-matter projection strength.
ocar.future_work: The technical report offers confidence for interpreting human DWI weights, while still leaving species and parcellation differences for later work.

summaries.beginner: Brain scans that follow water flow are used to guess how strongly two regions are wired, but that guess needed a check against chemical tracers in monkeys. In ten macaques, the scan-based counts rose and fell together with the tracer-based strengths.
summaries.intermediate: In Human Brain Mapping (2015), van den Heuvel and colleagues compare diffusion-MRI streamline counts and densities in 10 rhesus macaques with CoCoMac and Markov–Kennedy tract-tracing weights. Both DWI metrics correlated positively with tracing strength (P < 0.001 in each dataset). They argue NOS is a valid assessment of projection strength for in vivo connectomes.
summaries.advanced: Correlation is not identity: DWI can still miss or invent pathways. n=10 macaques; P values do not convey effect size. CoCoMac is a collated literature database with known inconsistencies. Catalog organism is “other”; stages include proofreading, infrastructure, and graph_analysis.

plain_language_summary: Brain scans that follow water flow are used to guess how strongly two regions are wired, but that guess needed a check against chemical tracers in monkeys. In ten macaques, the scan-based counts rose and fell together with the tracer-based strengths.

ocar.opportunity: If a connectome is a complete map of anatomical and functional connectivity, it should include glia, which shape wiring from whole-brain networks down to synaptic nanodomains.
ocar.challenge: Most connectome programs still center neurons, leaving glial contributions to anatomy and function under-specified.
ocar.action: Fields, Woo, and Basser survey glial interactions with the neuronal connectome across long-range networks, local circuits, and individual synapses, and highlight research opportunities.
ocar.resolution: The perspective argues that understanding neuronal connectivity is incomplete without all glial types, from single synapses to circuits.
ocar.future_work: They explicitly flag opportunities for future research on how glia define and regulate anatomical and functional connectivity.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps usually follow nerve cells, but support cells called glia also shape those connections. This perspective argues that a full wiring diagram has to include glia, from tiny synapses up to whole-brain networks.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2015), Fields, Woo, and Basser argue that glia belong in the connectome because they regulate connectivity across length scales. The article is a perspective, not a new dataset, catalogued under biological application without a specific organism or method tag.
summaries.advanced: No new experiments or quantified glial connectomes are presented. The piece is programmatic. Catalog stages are empty; treat claims as a research agenda.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps usually follow nerve cells, but support cells called glia also shape those connections. This perspective argues that a full wiring diagram has to include glia, from tiny synapses up to whole-brain networks.

ocar.opportunity: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas provides mesoscale axonal projections for C57Bl/6J mice in a common 3D space, as a quantitative, open database of inter-areal and cell-type-specific pathways.
ocar.challenge: Meaningful quantification depends on a high-fidelity template, precise mapping of raw data, accurate signal detection, connection-strength algorithms, and usable web presentation.
ocar.action: Kuan, Zeng, Hawrylycz, Ng and colleagues describe key informatics pipeline steps that created the atlas and illustrate basic application use cases.
ocar.resolution: They present the atlas’s standardized platform, public portal (connectivity.brain-map.org), and the informatics choices that make quantified comparison possible.
ocar.future_work: Use cases in the paper are meant to guide further analysis of the public resource rather than close the mesoscale map.

summaries.beginner: A large public atlas traces outgoing cables from many starting points in the mouse brain and places them in one 3D map. This paper explains the computer pipeline that turns those pictures into numbers scientists can compare.
summaries.intermediate: In Methods (2015), Kuan and Allen Institute colleagues describe informatics behind the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas: template and framework, registration, signal detection, quantitative strength, and the open website. The atlas uses a standardized platform for C57Bl/6J mesoscale projections. Catalog organism is mouse; stage is infrastructure.
summaries.advanced: This is a pipeline/methods paper, not a biological discovery article. Connection “strength” is optical-signal-based, not EM synapse counts. Template fidelity and detection thresholds are the main caveats for downstream users.

plain_language_summary: A large public atlas traces outgoing cables from many starting points in the mouse brain and places them in one 3D map. This paper explains the computer pipeline that turns those pictures into numbers scientists can compare.

ocar.opportunity: Finding important nodes in biological networks could highlight control points, conserved regulators, and targets for networked medicine.
ocar.challenge: Degree, betweenness, and PageRank capture different aspects of undirected graphs, and few importance measures were tailored to directed biological networks.
ocar.action: Wang, Lü, and Yu propose a measure based on network motifs and principal component analysis and test it on five real-world biological networks.
