ocar.resolution: A single session can zoom from mesoscale to super-resolution, revealing mitotic cleavage planes and alignment of pre- and postsynaptic proteins in mature human brain organoids imaged in toto down to synaptic resolution.
ocar.future_work: They expect LSFEM to aid qualitative and quantitative organoid studies in development and disease.

summaries.beginner: Mini-brains grown from human cells are thick, so seeing both the whole structure and the tiniest synapses is hard. The authors swell the tissue and use a sheet of light to image the entire organoid, then zoom in to synaptic detail in the same session.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Rodriguez-Gatica, Brüstle, Schwarz, Kubitscheck and colleagues combine expansion microscopy with light-sheet imaging of human brain organoids. LSFEM spans meso- to nanoscale, including cleavage-plane geometry and pre-/postsynaptic protein alignment, and images mature organoids in toto at synaptic resolution. Catalog methods include expansion microscopy, light-sheet, and super-resolution LM; stage is alignment.
summaries.advanced: Expansion factor, labeling panels, and quantitative error versus EM are not in the abstract. “Synaptic resolution” refers to aligned synaptic proteins, not EM-verified synapses. Organoid-to-in vivo correspondence remains a general caveat.

plain_language_summary: Mini-brains grown from human cells are thick, so seeing both the whole structure and the tiniest synapses is hard. The authors swell the tissue and use a sheet of light to image the entire organoid, then zoom in to synaptic detail in the same session.

ocar.opportunity: Higher-order thalamic neurons receive layer 5 drive from cortex and project back, forming a transthalamic route for corticocortical communication, so a single relay cell might mix different cortical messages.
ocar.challenge: Whether individual posterior medial nucleus cells integrate layer 5 input from distinct cortical areas, such as somatosensory versus motor, was unknown at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Sampathkumar, Sherman, Kasthuri and colleagues combined genetic dual labeling of sensory and motor layer 5 synapses with serial EM connectomics in mice.
ocar.resolution: Significant convergence occurred on 19 of 33 reconstructed thalamic cells. As a population, layer 5 synapses were larger and more proximal on dendrites than unlabeled synapses. Many or most of these neurons therefore integrate signals as disparate as sensory and motor cortex rather than merely relaying one afferent stream.
ocar.future_work: The result adds complexity to higher-order thalamic function in overall cortical processing, motivating further dual-label EM in other nuclei.

summaries.beginner: Some thalamic cells sit between cortical areas and might simply pass along one message. In mice, more than half of the reconstructed cells in one higher-order nucleus received large, close-in synapses from both sensory and motor cortex, suggesting they mix those messages.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2021), Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri use dual genetic labeling plus serial EM to distinguish somatosensory versus motor layer 5 synapses onto mouse posterior medial nucleus cells. Convergence was significant on 19 of 33 reconstructed neurons; layer 5 terminals were larger and more proximal than unlabeled synapses. Catalog method is electron microscopy; axis is biological_application.
summaries.advanced: n=33 reconstructed cells is modest; “19 of 33” is the key fraction. Unlabeled synapses are a mixed remainder class. “Significant convergence” should be read with the paper’s statistics. Only POm and these two cortical origins are tested.

plain_language_summary: Some thalamic cells sit between cortical areas and might simply pass along one message. In mice, more than half of the reconstructed cells in one higher-order nucleus received large, close-in synapses from both sensory and motor cortex, suggesting they mix those messages.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric brain imaging now produces enormous 3D data from which neuronal morphometry—somata, dendrites, axons, and potential synapses—can be reconstructed for cell typing and connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Doing this at high quality across petabyte-scale whole-brain databases is extremely challenging for data and workflow management.
ocar.action: Jiang, Peng and colleagues developed a multi-level method on a petabyte hardware/software platform to generate somatic, dendritic, axonal, and putative synaptic morphometry, including tools for sharing and remote collaborative validation.
ocar.resolution: In 62 whole mouse brains they identified 50,233 somata, profiled dendrites of 11,322 neurons, fully reconstructed 1,050 neurons (dendrites plus full axons), and detected 1.9 million putative synaptic sites from axonal boutons. Analysis and simulation indicate promise for large-scale morphology applications.
ocar.future_work: The platform is presented to enable further whole-brain morphometry at this scale.

summaries.beginner: Modern whole-brain microscopes create so much data that tracing cells becomes a computing problem as much as a biology problem. This team processed dozens of mouse brains and produced tens of thousands of cell bodies, over a thousand full neuron shapes, and millions of possible contact sites.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroinformatics (2021), Jiang, Yimin Wang, Hanchuan Peng and colleagues report petabyte-scale multi-morphometry across 62 whole mouse brains: 50,233 somata, dendritic profiles of 11,322 neurons, 1,050 full axon-and-dendrite reconstructions, and 1.9 million putative bouton-derived synaptic sites. Catalog organism is mouse; stages are infrastructure and modeling.
summaries.advanced: Putative synapses from boutons are not EM-verified contacts. Full reconstructions (1,050) are a subset of identified somata (50,233). “Petabyte-scale” describes the database, not a single image’s size. Collaborative validation is claimed as a workflow feature.

plain_language_summary: Modern whole-brain microscopes create so much data that tracing cells becomes a computing problem as much as a biology problem. This team processed dozens of mouse brains and produced tens of thousands of cell bodies, over a thousand full neuron shapes, and millions of possible contact sites.

ocar.opportunity: Animals rapidly adapt movements to perturbations, with parallel changes in motor-cortex activity, but whether those changes come from altered inputs (Hinput) or local connectivity (Hlocal) is hard to test because synapses cannot easily be measured in vivo.
ocar.challenge: Preserved neural covariance during adaptation has been taken to favor Hinput, because stable covariance was presumed to require preserved local connectivity.
ocar.action: Feulner, Clopath and colleagues used a modular recurrent neural network to compare Hinput versus Hlocal qualitatively, then simulated tasks demanding larger behavioral changes.
ocar.resolution: Hinput yielded small activity changes and largely preserved covariance, as expected. Surprisingly, Hlocal needed only small, correlated connectivity changes and produced only slightly larger activity and covariance shifts, still within experimental ranges. Larger behavioral change widened the Hinput–Hlocal gap, a possible future experimental design.
ocar.future_work: They propose exploiting tasks with larger behavioral change to distinguish input-driven versus local-plasticity accounts.

summaries.beginner: When you quickly adjust a movement, motor-cortex activity changes, but it is hard to know if the local wiring changed. A computer network shows that tiny, coordinated rewiring can change behavior while leaving activity statistics looking almost as if the wiring stayed put.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2021), Feulner, Perich, Chowdhury, Miller, Gallego, and Clopath compare input versus local-connectivity hypotheses of rapid motor adaptation in modular RNNs. Local plasticity can succeed with small correlated weight changes that largely preserve covariance, overlapping experimental observations. Bigger behavioral demands increase the difference between the two hypotheses. Catalog stage is modeling.
summaries.advanced: This is a qualitative RNN study, not in vivo synaptic measurements. “Within the range of experimental recordings” refers to activity/covariance, not proof that cortex uses Hlocal. No organism is tagged. Task design for future experiments is the main empirical proposal.

plain_language_summary: When you quickly adjust a movement, motor-cortex activity changes, but it is hard to know if the local wiring changed. A computer network shows that tiny, coordinated rewiring can change behavior while leaving activity statistics looking almost as if the wiring stayed put.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic connectivity patterns underlie brain function, so recognition molecules that decide where and when synapses form are fundamental to cellular neuroscience.
ocar.challenge: Partner choice, rejection of incorrect partners, synapse specification, and removal of inappropriate synapses involve many protein families whose logic is still being parsed.
ocar.action: Chowdhury, Watters, and Biederer review adhesion and signaling complexes and secreted factors in vertebrate synaptic partner recognition, following a developmental sequence and highlighting Cadherins, immunoglobulin superfamily, Semaphorins/Plexins, LRR proteins, and Neurexins plus binders.
ocar.resolution: They define diversifying themes—cell-type-specific expression, combinatorial action, alternative splicing, post-translational modification—and discuss proteomics, single-cell expression, and laminated structures such as hippocampus and retina (catalog DS09/DS10 mouse retina) as advantageous systems. They stress disease relevance for neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.
ocar.future_work: An outlook lists research goals for explaining the precision and diversity of synaptic connections.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells use molecular name-tags to decide whom to connect with, whom to avoid, and which extra connections to prune. This chapter reviews those molecules and why mistakes in the system matter for developmental and psychiatric disease.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Topics in Developmental Biology (2021), Chowdhury, Watters, and Biederer review vertebrate synaptic recognition molecules across wiring, rejection, specification, and elimination. Key families include cadherins, Ig superfamily, Semaphorin/Plexin, LRR proteins, and neurexins. They highlight combinatorial codes, splicing, and laminated circuits such as retina. Catalog organism is mouse; stage is synapses.
summaries.advanced: This is a chapter-length review, not new connectivity data. Catalog dataset DS09/DS10 reflects retinal examples, not a restriction of the review’s scope. Disease links are discussed as profound but not newly mapped here.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells use molecular name-tags to decide whom to connect with, whom to avoid, and which extra connections to prune. This chapter reviews those molecules and why mistakes in the system matter for developmental and psychiatric disease.

ocar.opportunity: The adult zebrafish pallium (dorsal telencephalic area D) is subdivided into medial, lateral, dorsal, central, anterior, and posterior zones whose interconnectivity and extrapallial links needed a hodological (connectional) synthesis.
ocar.challenge: Without a comprehensive connection map, homology and functional modularity of teleost pallial regions remain hard to compare with other species and with developmental genetic studies.
ocar.action: Yáñez, Anadón and colleagues used carbocyanine tracing and ancillary anatomy to map the adult zebrafish pallial connectome (catalog DS15 zebrafish).
ocar.resolution: Interconnectivity among pallial areas is poor, especially among Dm, Dl/Dd, and Dp, suggesting dedicated modules, and extrapallial afferents are similarly compartmentalized (preglomerular, posterior tuberal, lateral recess, and subpallial sources). Efferents are region-characteristic: Dc receives from Dl–Dd and projects to pretectum and tectum, Dp interconnects with olfactory bulbs, and rostral Dm projects to the dorsal entopeduncular nucleus.
ocar.future_work: They present the connectome as a complement to neuroanatomy and as a reference for early-stage neurogenetic studies, and they compare it with other teleosts given high pallial diversity.

summaries.beginner: The zebrafish’s pallium is divided into several neighborhoods that turn out not to talk to each other very much. Dye-tracing shows each neighborhood has its own incoming and outgoing routes, like separate work units rather than one fully mixed network.
summaries.intermediate: In The Journal of comparative neurology (2021), Yáñez, Folgueira, Lamas, and Anadón map adult zebrafish pallial connections with carbocyanine tracers. Poor inter-area mixing, especially Dm versus Dl/Dd versus Dp, supports modular organization. They detail preglomerular, posterior tuberal, lateral recess, and subpallial inputs and region-specific outputs, including Dc to pretectum/tectum. Catalog dataset is DS15 zebrafish.
summaries.advanced: Hodology here is tracer-based, not EM-synapse resolution. “Poor interconnectivity” is qualitative. Teleost pallial homology remains debated; the paper compares other teleosts but cannot settle mammalian homologies. Catalog stages are proofreading and graph_analysis.

plain_language_summary: The zebrafish’s pallium is divided into several neighborhoods that turn out not to talk to each other very much. Dye-tracing shows each neighborhood has its own incoming and outgoing routes, like separate work units rather than one fully mixed network.

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical function depends on bidirectional communication with thalamus through cortico-thalamo-cortical (CTC) loops, and cell-type-specific synaptic mapping is clarifying their organization across sensory, motor, and cognitive areas.
ocar.challenge: The puzzle is how simple and complex CTC loops, interlinked with local and corticocortical circuits, plus embedded inhibition, jointly support communication across hierarchical networks and phenomena such as consciousness and perception.
ocar.action: Shepherd and Yamawaki review cell-type-specific connections among major cortical and thalamic neurons, outline general versus specialized loop features, and relate CTC loops to established CTC and CC models.
ocar.resolution: They propose CTC–CC loop chains as a modular organizational unit and scaffolding for area-specific modifications, with inhibitory circuits shaping excitation flow throughout.
ocar.future_work: They highlight efforts to pinpoint cell-type-specific CTC mechanisms in consciousness and perception as connectivity pieces fall into place.

summaries.beginner: Cortex and thalamus talk in loops, not one-way lines. This review assembles how different cell types in those loops are wired, and how chains of loops might be a repeating building block of large-scale brain communication.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2021), Shepherd and Yamawaki synthesize cell-type-specific CTC connectivity across areas. They distinguish simple versus complex loops, general versus specialized features, and coupling to corticocortical circuits, proposing CTC–CC loop chains as modular scaffolding. Inhibition is embedded throughout. Catalog stages are preparation and infrastructure; dimension is image-acquisition in the catalog despite being a circuit review.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; no new EM dataset is presented. Consciousness/perception links are a stated research frontier, not demonstrated here. Catalog method is empty. Area-specific modifications mean principles are not identical everywhere.

plain_language_summary: Cortex and thalamus talk in loops, not one-way lines. This review assembles how different cell types in those loops are wired, and how chains of loops might be a repeating building block of large-scale brain communication.

ocar.opportunity: Detailed conductance-based neurons with thousands of synapses are key for single-cell and network computation, and for interpreting experiments, including micro-connectomic networks and biologically inspired deep nets.
ocar.challenge: Simulating those models is computationally expensive, limiting their use.
ocar.action: Amsalem, Segev and colleagues introduce Neuron_Reduce, an analytical reduction that maps synapses and active channels onto a simplified morphology while preserving transfer impedance to the soma and merging synapses that share impedance into one NEURON process (keeping individual activation times).
ocar.resolution: For various cell types with 10,000–100,000 synapses, simulations accelerated 40–250-fold while closely replicating voltage dynamics and specific dendritic computations. The reduced models are public and straightforward to implement.
ocar.future_work: They expect the reductions to enable unprecedented-scale network simulations from micro-connectomics.

summaries.beginner: Realistic computer neurons with tens of thousands of inputs are too slow to simulate in large numbers. This method simplifies each cell’s shape while keeping how signals reach the cell body, speeding simulations tens to hundreds of times without wrecking the electrical behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2020), Amsalem, Eyal, Segev and colleagues present Neuron_Reduce. Synapses and active conductances are mapped by transfer impedance to the soma; identical-impedance synapses merge but keep separate spike times. Speedups of 40–250× are reported for several cell types with 10,000–100,000 synapses, with close voltage and dendritic-computation match. Catalog stages are infrastructure and modeling.
summaries.advanced: “Closely replicating” is qualitative in the abstract; which dendritic computations survive is named only as a class. Merging synapses assumes linear impedance equivalence that may fail for strongly nonlinear local spikes. No organism is tagged. Public implementation should be version-checked.

plain_language_summary: Realistic computer neurons with tens of thousands of inputs are too slow to simulate in large numbers. This method simplifies each cell’s shape while keeping how signals reach the cell body, speeding simulations tens to hundreds of times without wrecking the electrical behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Insect mushroom bodies are multisensory learning and memory centers; the honeybee calyx is comparatively large and receives olfactory, visual, and gustatory/tactile input.
ocar.challenge: Relating behavioral plasticity after brood care, sensory exposure, or associative long-term memory to identified synaptic microcircuits, and to physiology of those microcircuits, needs a synthesis of structure and function.
ocar.action: Groh and Rössler review plasticity of honeybee MB-calyx microglomeruli, focusing on synapses between sensory projection neurons and Kenyon cells, and compare selected aspects with other insects.
ocar.resolution: Structural plasticity of microglomeruli in olfactory and visual calyx compartments tracks those behavioral experiences, and physiological studies show learning-related changes in calyx microcircuit responses.
ocar.future_work: They highlight open questions and routes toward causal links between neuronal and behavioral plasticity in this social insect.

summaries.beginner: Honeybees learn smells and sights using a brain region packed with tiny repeating connection clusters. This review updates how those clusters change when bees are reared differently, see different worlds, or form long-term memories.
summaries.intermediate: In Insects (2020), Groh and Rössler review synaptic microcircuits in the honeybee mushroom-body calyx, especially projection-neuron to Kenyon-cell microglomeruli. Differential brood care, sensory exposure, and associative LTM associate with structural plasticity in olfactory and visual compartments, paralleled by physiological response changes. Catalog axis is biological_application.
summaries.advanced: This is a review of honeybee (and comparative insect) work, not a new EM connectome. Causal structure–behavior links remain an explicit open question. Catalog organism and method are empty despite Apis mellifera being the focus.

plain_language_summary: Honeybees learn smells and sights using a brain region packed with tiny repeating connection clusters. This review updates how those clusters change when bees are reared differently, see different worlds, or form long-term memories.

ocar.opportunity: In Parkinson’s disease, fibrillar α-synuclein is hypothesized to propagate through synaptically coupled networks, producing Lewy pathology; uptake and spread should then depend on neuronal phenotype and connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Rigorous comparison of spreading with anterograde and retrograde maps, including cell-type selectivity, was incomplete.
ocar.action: Henrich, Surmeier and colleagues injected preformed α-synuclein fibrils into mouse pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN)—a region that shows Lewy pathology in patients—and compared pathology with connectomic mapping of PPN.
ocar.resolution: Within PPN, pathology was cell-specific: robust in PD-vulnerable cholinergic neurons, not neighboring noncholinergics. Nearly all neurons projecting to PPN cholinergics developed pathology, but kinetics, magnitude, and persistence were unrelated to connection strength. Thus phenotype governs somatodendritic uptake, and the afferent connectome restricts spread without making burden a strict function of coupling strength.
ocar.future_work: The dissociation of strength versus permissiveness is a constraint for models of synuclein propagation.

summaries.beginner: Parkinson’s-related protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, the clumps preferred one cell type in a brainstem region and then appeared in cells that connect to it, but how much wiring those cells had did not simply predict how bad the clumps got.
summaries.intermediate: In Science Advances (2020), Henrich, Geibl, Dawson, Oertel, Surmeier and colleagues seed α-synuclein fibrils in mouse PPN. Cholinergic PPN neurons were selectively vulnerable; almost all afferents to those cells showed pathology, yet amount and persistence did not track connection strength from anterograde/retrograde maps. Catalog organism is mouse; axis is health_translation.
summaries.advanced: PPN injection site and mouse seeding are not identical to human PD progression. “Nearly all” afferents and “unrelated to strength” are the key quantitative-style claims without numeric correlation coefficients in the abstract. Phenotype versus connectome is a dual-factor conclusion.

plain_language_summary: Parkinson’s-related protein clumps are thought to hop along brain wiring. In mice, the clumps preferred one cell type in a brainstem region and then appeared in cells that connect to it, but how much wiring those cells had did not simply predict how bad the clumps got.

ocar.opportunity: Differential binding among related protein-family members can underlie cell–cell recognition, including DIP/Dpr immunoglobulin-like adhesion proteins that control synaptic connectivity in Drosophila.
ocar.challenge: How specificity is coded on a shared canonical DIP/Dpr interface, rather than wholly different binding modes, needed a sequence–structure–energy account.
ocar.action: Sergeeva, Honig and colleagues combined computational analysis with experimental affinity measurements, showing DIPs/Dprs form seven specificity subgroups by binding preference.
ocar.resolution: Subgroup specificity is controlled by “negative constraints” that interfere with non-cognate binding. Each subgroup uses a different combination of constraints distributed across most of the interface. They discuss structural origins of those constraints and possible general implications for multi-protein family specificity.
ocar.future_work: Generalization of negative-constraint logic to other adhesion families is posed as a broader implication.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly nerve cells choose partners using related stickiness proteins that look alike but do not all bind one another. Specificity comes less from a unique handshake and more from extra features that block the wrong pairings.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2020), Sergeeva, Katsamba, Shapiro, Honig and colleagues show Drosophila DIP/Dpr proteins fall into seven specificity subgroups. A computational plus affinity approach finds that negative constraints across the shared interface prevent non-cognate binding, with each subgroup using a different constraint combination. Catalog organism is fly; stage is segmentation.
summaries.advanced: Seven subgroups are a binding-preference classification, not a full in vivo connectivity proof for every pair. Catalog stage “segmentation” does not reflect the biochemistry focus. Evolutionary “design” is interpretive language for family-wide specificity rules.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly nerve cells choose partners using related stickiness proteins that look alike but do not all bind one another. Specificity comes less from a unique handshake and more from extra features that block the wrong pairings.

ocar.opportunity: Associative memories are classically stored in assemblies of strongly interconnected neurons that are assumed to comprise the same cells over time, yet synapses and neural representations change spontaneously.
ocar.challenge: How memories and behaviors persist if assemblies remodel completely is a conundrum.
ocar.action: Kossio, Memmesheimer and colleagues propose assemblies that drift via noisy activity and synaptic turnover, with teacher-free activity-dependent and homeostatic plasticity compensating the exchange so inputs, outputs, and assemblies stay consistent.
ocar.resolution: Gradual neuron exchange with compensatory plasticity conserves representational structure and yields persistent memory. The model explains experimental temporal evolution of fear-memory representations and shows drifting assemblies can still support stable memories and basic computations.
ocar.future_work: They suggest drift-and-compensation mechanisms may apply to other drifting neural representations.

summaries.beginner: Memories are often pictured as a fixed club of tightly linked cells, but real connections keep changing. This theory says the club’s membership can slowly turn over while simple learning rules keep the memory usable.
summaries.intermediate: In work listed as PNAS 2020 (DOI 10.1101/2020.08.31.276147), Kossio, Goedeke, Klos, and Memmesheimer model freely drifting assemblies. Spontaneous synaptic change and noisy activity exchange neurons; unsupervised plasticity conserves structure so memory persists. They relate this to evolving fear-memory representations. Catalog stage is infrastructure.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical/modeling paper; fear-memory experiments are cited as explananda, not newly performed here. Complete remodeling is a modeling regime. Catalog journal/DOI mismatch (PNAS versus bioRxiv prefix) should be checked at the landing URL. No organism tag.

plain_language_summary: Memories are often pictured as a fixed club of tightly linked cells, but real connections keep changing. This theory says the club’s membership can slowly turn over while simple learning rules keep the memory usable.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics, transcriptomics, and physiology now make brain-wide circuits tractable, yet neocortical areas look like repetitions of a canonical local circuit while supporting diverse functions.
ocar.challenge: Area differences in biological properties were often treated as random heterogeneity rather than organized variation.
ocar.action: Xiao-Jing Wang reviews evidence that synaptic excitation and inhibition display systematic macroscopic gradients across cortex, including abnormalities in mental illness, and that quantitative gradient differences can yield qualitatively new dynamics via bifurcations.
ocar.resolution: Combined with evolution, development, and plasticity, gradients plus bifurcations are proposed as a generative principle of large-scale cortical functional diversity aligned with hierarchy.
ocar.future_work: The perspective frames this principle as a research program for linking measured gradients to hierarchical function.

summaries.beginner: Different patches of the brain’s outer layer are not identical copies of one circuit. This perspective argues that smoothly changing strengths of excitation and inhibition across the cortex can make those patches behave in qualitatively different ways.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2020), Xiao-Jing Wang proposes that macroscopic gradients of synaptic excitation and inhibition, aligned with cortical hierarchy, generate functional diversity through nonlinear bifurcations. Gradients are described as abnormal in mental illness. Catalog axis is biological_application; this is a perspective, not a new map.
summaries.advanced: No new gradient measurements appear in the abstract. Bifurcation is a mathematical mechanism, not a demonstrated clinical pathway. “Mental illness” is named without specific disorders or effect sizes here.

plain_language_summary: Different patches of the brain’s outer layer are not identical copies of one circuit. This perspective argues that smoothly changing strengths of excitation and inhibition across the cortex can make those patches behave in qualitatively different ways.

ocar.opportunity: Imaging neurons and circuits over large volumes at high speed and subcellular resolution would let researchers watch activity in dendrites, spines, and ensembles across distant cortical regions.
ocar.challenge: Standard two-photon imaging struggles to combine mesoscale fields, volumetric rate, and synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Lu, Ji and colleagues incorporated a Bessel focus module into a two-photon fluorescence mesoscope.
ocar.resolution: The system enabled rapid volumetric calcium imaging with synaptic resolution, including entire dendritic spans and neural ensembles in multiple cortical regions over two hemispheres of the awake mouse brain, covering soma, dendrites, and spines.
ocar.future_work: The technology is presented for further mesoscale activity mapping; additional indicators or species are not claimed in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Watching many brain cells fire, including the tiny spines on their branches, across a wide area is usually too slow or too blurry. Adding a special focus shape to a two-photon microscope let the authors film activity over large stretches of an awake mouse’s cortex at that fine scale.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2020), Lu, Liang, Meng, Zhou, Svoboda, Paninski, and Na Ji add a Bessel focus to a two-photon mesoscope for rapid volumetric imaging at synaptic resolution. They demonstrate calcium imaging of full dendritic arbors and ensembles across multiple cortical areas and both hemispheres in awake mouse. Catalog method is two-photon; organism is mouse; axis is biological_application.
summaries.advanced: “Synaptic resolution” here is optical (spines), not EM. The abstract does not give volume size, Hertz rate, or number of neurons. Awake mouse cortex is the demonstrated preparation.

plain_language_summary: Watching many brain cells fire, including the tiny spines on their branches, across a wide area is usually too slow or too blurry. Adding a special focus shape to a two-photon microscope let the authors film activity over large stretches of an awake mouse’s cortex at that fine scale.

ocar.opportunity: The brain’s computational power and its vulnerability to injury depend on dense synaptic microconnectivity, which has been hard to quantify at scale in animals and humans.
ocar.challenge: Synapses are small and tightly packed, and mapping them often required laborious large histological arrays.
ocar.action: Sauerbeck, Holtzman and colleagues developed SEQUIN, a super-resolution imaging and analysis workflow that identifies, quantifies, and molecularly characterizes central synapses for automated volumetric mesoscale mapping.
ocar.resolution: SEQUIN revealed delayed cortical synapse loss after diffuse traumatic brain injury. Similar loss appeared in an Alzheimer-disease model, where excitatory-synapse mapping across hippocampus showed region-specific vulnerability. They propose synaptopathy as a mechanistic link between Alzheimer neurodegeneration and brain trauma, its best-established epigenetic risk factor.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered for broader nano-to-mesoscale synapse quantification in models and human tissue.

summaries.beginner: Counting the brain’s connection points over a large area usually takes enormous labor. A new super-resolution pipeline, SEQUIN, does that more automatically and finds that both head injury and an Alzheimer’s model lose synapses, in overlapping ways.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2020), Sauerbeck and colleagues introduce SEQUIN for super-resolution LM synapse mapping without large histological arrays. They report delayed cortical synapse loss after diffuse TBI and region-specific hippocampal excitatory synapse loss in an AD model, arguing for a synaptopathy link between trauma and Alzheimer neurodegeneration. Catalog method is super-resolution LM; axis is biological_application.
summaries.advanced: SEQUIN characterizes putative synapses optically/molecularly, not by EM. “Delayed” loss is not given a time in the abstract. Human applicability is claimed in the workflow description; the highlighted biology is animal TBI and an AD model. “Epigenetic risk factor” wording is the authors’ framing of trauma’s relation to AD.

plain_language_summary: Counting the brain’s connection points over a large area usually takes enormous labor. A new super-resolution pipeline, SEQUIN, does that more automatically and finds that both head injury and an Alzheimer’s model lose synapses, in overlapping ways.

ocar.opportunity: Sex-specific synaptic connectivity is an emerging, underexplored feature of animal brains, and Doublesex/Mab-3 related transcription factors (DMRTs) are candidates to control it.
ocar.challenge: How a conserved DMRT could act only in one sex, including via posttranslational control, was unclear for C. elegans phasmid neurons.
ocar.action: Bayer, Oren-Suissa, Hobert and colleagues analyzed dmd-4, a previously uncharacterized DMRT, in sex-shared phasmid sensory neurons.
ocar.resolution: dmd-4 is expressed in two phasmid classes in hermaphrodites but not males, and it promotes hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connectivity and function. Sex specificity arises from sex-specific protein stabilization via ubiquitin binding to the conserved DMA domain. A human DMRT homolog is controlled similarly, suggesting wider relevance.
ocar.future_work: Implications for sexual differentiation in other animals are explicitly suggested via the human homolog result.

summaries.beginner: Male and female roundworms can wire the same sensory cells differently. A gene-control protein present in females but not males is kept stable by a small protein tag, and that stability helps build the female connection pattern; a related human protein appears to be controlled the same way.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Bayer, Hobert, Oren-Suissa and colleagues show that C. elegans dmd-4 is hermaphrodite-specific in two phasmid neuron classes (catalog DS01) and is required for their sex-specific synapses and function. DMA-domain ubiquitin binding stabilizes DMD-4 in a sex-specific manner. A human DMRT homolog is similarly controlled. Catalog organism is elegans.
summaries.advanced: Two phasmid classes are the expression focus, not a whole-brain DMRT map. Human control “in a similar manner” is a biochemical/cell-system claim to inspect, not a human circuit result. Catalog axis is registry_dataset.

plain_language_summary: Male and female roundworms can wire the same sensory cells differently. A gene-control protein present in females but not males is kept stable by a small protein tag, and that stability helps build the female connection pattern; a related human protein appears to be controlled the same way.

ocar.opportunity: Relating interneuronal correlations to synaptic structure is a core problem; balanced networks can produce an “asynchronous state” with very weak spike correlations.
ocar.challenge: Prior theory assumed uncorrelated feedforward spike trains, whereas cortex receives correlated input, which may create a different correlated regime.
ocar.action: Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum analyze balanced networks driven by correlated feedforward spike trains.
ocar.resolution: Correlated feedforward input produces much larger downstream correlations—a “correlated state”—with tight excitatory–inhibitory balance matching in vivo cortical recordings, unlike the asynchronous state.
ocar.future_work: The implied use is interpreting cortical correlation structure when input correlations cannot be neglected.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells’ firing can be almost independent or can rise and fall together. Theory that assumes incoming spikes are independent misses a regime in which shared incoming chatter makes the local network both tightly balanced and more correlated, closer to real cortex.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review E (2019), Baker, Ebsch, Lampl, and Rosenbaum show that balanced networks receiving correlated feedforward spikes enter a correlated state with much larger pairwise correlations and tight E/I balance, unlike asynchronous-state theory with uncorrelated input. Catalog axis is bridge; stage is graph_analysis.
summaries.advanced: This is theory plus comparison to in vivo-like balance, not a new connectome. “Much larger” correlations are not given numerically in the abstract. Architecture beyond balance and feedforward correlation structure is not fully specified here.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells’ firing can be almost independent or can rise and fall together. Theory that assumes incoming spikes are independent misses a regime in which shared incoming chatter makes the local network both tightly balanced and more correlated, closer to real cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Lipids build cells and organelles, but nanoscale lipid imaging has been largely limited to electron microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Optical nanoscale imaging of membranes, together with protein labels, needed a lipid-compatible expansion-microscopy chemistry.
ocar.action: Karagiannis, Boyden, Kasthuri and colleagues introduce and validate a chemical tag enabling membrane expansion microscopy (mExM), plus a post-expansion antibody labeling protocol.
ocar.resolution: mExM visualizes protein–lipid relationships in mitochondria, ER, nuclear envelope, and Golgi. They suggest uses in cell–cell interactions, intracellular transport, and neural connectomics. Catalog methods include expansion microscopy and electron microscopy (as the comparison/context).
ocar.future_work: Proposed applications in connectomics and organelle biology are use cases, not completed circuit maps.

summaries.beginner: Cell membranes are made of fats that are hard to see with ordinary light microscopes at tiny scales. A new chemical tag lets those membranes swell with expansion microscopy so proteins and lipids can be imaged together in organelles.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Karagiannis, Kang, Shin, Boyden, Kasthuri and colleagues present mExM, a lipid-optimized expansion-microscopy method with a validated membrane tag and post-expansion antibody labeling. They image membranes and proteins in mitochondria, ER, nuclear membrane, and Golgi, and discuss connectomic uses. Catalog axis is biological_application.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint. Expansion fidelity for lipids versus proteins can differ; the abstract claims validation but not numeric distortion metrics. Connectomics is a suggested application. EM is listed as a catalog method (context), not as the imaging mode of mExM.

plain_language_summary: Cell membranes are made of fats that are hard to see with ordinary light microscopes at tiny scales. A new chemical tag lets those membranes swell with expansion microscopy so proteins and lipids can be imaged together in organelles.

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical synaptic connectivity has first-order structure (pairwise statistics such as cell-type strengths and distance dependence) and higher-order structure (for example abundant all-to-all cliques).
ocar.challenge: The relative impact of first- versus higher-order structure on emergent activity is unknown, and two microcircuit models can share first-order statistics while differing in higher-order topology.
ocar.action: Nolte, Gal, Markram, and Reimann compared two neocortical microcircuit models with similar first-order connectivity, only one of which includes higher-order structure from morphological diversity within neuronal types.
ocar.resolution: Morphological diversity yielded more heterogeneous degree distributions, more cliques, and more small-world topology. Higher-order structure came with nuanced activity changes, including stronger dependence of pairwise correlations on neurons’ positions in cliques. Models with similar first-order wiring can thus differ drastically in higher-order structure, which appears to shape emergent activity.
ocar.future_work: The comparison argues that reconstructions ignoring within-type morphological diversity will miss activity-relevant topology.

summaries.beginner: Two computer cortices can have the same average “who connects to whom” statistics and still differ in larger wiring patterns such as fully connected cliques. Those extra patterns, which come from cells of the same type having different shapes, slightly change how activity lines up between cells.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Nolte, Gal, Markram, and Reimann compare neocortical microcircuit models that match first-order connectivity but differ in higher-order structure arising from morphological diversity within types. Diversity increased degree heterogeneity, clique counts, and small-worldness, and it altered correlation patterns depending on clique position. Catalog stage is graph_analysis.
summaries.advanced: This is a modeling comparison, not in vivo perturbation of morphology. “Nuanced” activity changes may be small relative to first-order effects; the abstract does not quantify effect sizes. Species/area of the microcircuit models are not named here (Blue Brain-style neocortex is the group’s usual setting).

plain_language_summary: Two computer cortices can have the same average “who connects to whom” statistics and still differ in larger wiring patterns such as fully connected cliques. Those extra patterns, which come from cells of the same type having different shapes, slightly change how activity lines up between cells.

ocar.opportunity: A multimodality effort now aims to identify and classify human brain networks with neurobiologically meaningful, computable measures—the human connectome—by placing anatomical and functional connections on the same map.
ocar.challenge: Methods are diverse (structural/functional MRI, EEG, MEG, non-invasive stimulation) and local versus global connectivity measures need expert synthesis, including for linking connectivity abnormalities to neuropsychiatric disorders.
ocar.action: After an IFCN-endorsed meeting, Rossini and an international panel review the state of the art on anatomical and functional connectivity methods and measures.
ocar.resolution: The document covers commonly used MRI, EEG, MEG, and non-invasive brain-stimulation techniques and local/global connectivity measures as a current knowledge survey for the human brain connectome.
ocar.future_work: The review is intended as a reference for applying these tools to structural–functional mechanisms and disease, not as a single recommended pipeline.

summaries.beginner: There are many ways to estimate how human brain regions are linked, from MRI to electrical recordings to stimulation. This expert review, sponsored by an international clinical neurophysiology group, surveys those methods and what they measure.
summaries.intermediate: In Clinical Neurophysiology (2019), Rossini and colleagues provide an IFCN-sponsored review of human connectome methods: anatomical and functional connectivity via structural/functional MRI, EEG, MEG, and non-invasive stimulation, plus local and global graph measures. Network analysis is presented as a tool for structure–function mechanisms and neuropsychiatric connectivity abnormalities. Catalog stage is graph_analysis.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review, not new empirical connectivity. Macroscopic imaging/physiology is not synaptic EM. Disease applications are motivational. No organism tag; the subject is human by title.

plain_language_summary: There are many ways to estimate how human brain regions are linked, from MRI to electrical recordings to stimulation. This expert review, sponsored by an international clinical neurophysiology group, surveys those methods and what they measure.
